title: To Scale Up or To Scale Out: Evaluating Space-Time Costs of Compiled Logical Circuits on Modular Superconducting Quantum Processors
authors: Nikiforos Paraskevopoulos, Sebastian de Bone, Mick Christophersen, Simon Storz, A. Mert Bozkurt, Arno Bargerbos, Sebastian Feld
abstract: Modular integration has emerged as the main pathway for scaling superconducting quantum processing units (QPUs) beyond the constraints of fabrication yield and physical footprint. Currently, two primary strategies lead this effort. Mirroring the "Scaling Up" and "Scaling Out" approaches in GPU architectures and AI infrastructures, these are: chiplet-based scaling, which preserves dense connectivity and high gate fidelity at the expense of engineering complexity, and distributed architectures, which decouple system scaling from monolithic QPU advancements at the expense of sparser connectivity and lower interconnect quality. To evaluate these approaches, we introduce a quantitative stress test measuring the execution cost of a dense workload of random logical entangling operations using a surface code scheme. Using a dedicated compiler, we compute the space-time cost as the number of network nodes increases, analysing this scaling behaviour across various surface code distances, Bell-state fidelities, and Bell-pair generation times. We find that distributed architectures incur an up to exponential space-time performance penalty compared to an effectively monolithic architecture across all simulations. Our results also show that as the network grows, this penalty manifests in two distinct scaling regimes: a noise-dominated regime constrained by insufficient Bell-state fidelity and generation rates, and a connectivity-dominated regime bottlenecked by lattice-surgery routing congestion.
summary: This paper analyzes the scaling challenges of building large quantum computers by comparing 'Scaling Up' (chiplet) versus 'Scaling Out' (distributed) superconducting architectures. Using a detailed compiler model, the authors find that distributed systems suffer severe performance penalties due to interconnect limitations. The work quantifies the trade-offs between connectivity, noise, and physical overhead in realizing fault-tolerant quantum computation.
main_problem: The paper evaluates the space-time costs associated with executing compiled logical quantum circuits when scaling superconducting quantum processors using either chiplet-based ('Scaling Up') or distributed ('Scaling Out') modular architectures.
main_result: Distributed architectures incur a significant, potentially exponential, space-time performance penalty compared to effectively monolithic designs, with this penalty manifesting in noise-limited and connectivity-limited regimes.
method: A quantitative stress test using a dedicated compiler calculates the space-time cost by simulating random logical entangling operations across varying network sizes and hardware parameters.
model_or_system: The study models superconducting Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) that employ the surface code for Quantum Error Correction (QEC). It compares the connectivity and error mechanisms of monolithic layouts versus those requiring inter-module links.

main_assumptions: The analysis assumes specific error models for bulk operations versus seam operations, and it probes a 'forward-looking parameter space' beyond current experimental limitations.

paper_structure: The paper develops the cost metric by first defining the physical constraints of scaling up vs. scaling out, then modeling the logical compilation process, and finally deriving and comparing the resulting space-time costs across different error regimes.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, quantitative framework for assessing the overhead associated with modularity in large-scale quantum computation, which is crucial for guiding hardware development in superconducting quantum computing.
